instruction: Compare the original and rewrite directly. Independently identify substantive reasoning relations in the original and check all against the rewrite, including omissions, additions, conditions, timing, actors, causal direction, and scope. Return status preserved only when all substantive reasoning survives. Use changed for a material change and uncertain for unresolved meaning. Give concrete evidence for your assessment. Wording and presentation order may differ. Give a short explanation referring to specific parts of the two texts.

documents.original:
Keep a pencil and reusable name cards by the rack so a maker can claim a board before a dozen similar bowls land beside it. If a shelf is too deep to reach across from one side, leave access behind it so nobody has to lean over a row of fresh rims. A small lamp aimed along the back of a dim shelf makes an empty spot easier to distinguish from a space occupied by a low dish. Leave an example board on the teaching table with the pots spaced for a hand to pass between them. Beginners can see how much room to allow before they load their own.

Keep empty boards on a separate stand near the worktables so students don't mistake a supply pile for occupied drying space. Let members nominate someone to check their work during an absence, giving staff a known person to ask if a piece needs attention.
documents.rewrite:
A student should be able to put their name on a board while they still know which of a dozen lookalike bowls is theirs. A pencil and a supply of reusable name cards right at the rack let them claim the board before the other bowls arrive. On the teaching table, set out a board of pots with enough space to slip a hand between neighbors. Beginners can use it to judge the gaps as they get ready to fill their own boards.

If a shelf is deeper than a person can comfortably reach, keep the space behind it clear so they can reach the far pots without leaning over freshly made rims. On a dark shelf, point a small light along the back so a low dish is easy to spot even where the shelf looks empty. Give spare boards their own stand by the worktables so students can tell supplies from work taking up drying space. Members who will be away can name someone to look in on their pots. Then staff know whom to ask if one needs attention.

documents.original:
Put the number of available chairs against each date on a shared booking calendar so organizers can see whether a request will fit. Have each organizer name someone reachable during the event. A driver running late can call the person with the keys. Give a chair with a loose hinge or missing foot a conspicuous repair tag and a separate storage spot, keeping it out of the next delivery. Provide a sheltered place to unfold wet returns and let them dry before they go back into storage.

Give the event team removable row signs that clip on. They can reserve seats without leaving tape or adhesive on borrowed chairs. Let a borrower nominate another person to make the return so the chairs can get back on time even when the event organizer has to leave early.
documents.rewrite:
An organizer looking up a date in the shared booking calendar should see how many chairs are free that day and be able to tell if there are enough for the event. Ask each organizer for the name of someone who can take a call and has the keys during the event, in case the delivery driver is delayed. When borrowers arrange the return, let them designate someone else to bring the chairs back. That keeps the agreed time workable even if the organizer leaves early.

Supply row signs the event team can clip on to reserve seats and take off afterward, so the borrowed chairs come back free of tape and sticky residue. If chairs come back wet, have a spot under cover where they can stand open until they're dry enough to store. Should a chair have a loose hinge or be missing a foot, put a repair tag where it's easy to see and store the chair separately so it won't go out with the next load.

documents.original:
Include a brief description of a meaningful sound, such as the train whistle both speakers stop to hear, when it helps explain their reaction. Break lines at natural points in a sentence and keep a person's first and last name together to make the text easier to take in at a glance. Ask a reviewer to follow a complete interview with the sound muted and flag places where a reply seems to come out of nowhere. Give visitors a correction slip with space for the interview title and playback time so staff can find a reported error.

Introduce a recorded letter or diary excerpt in the captions when a narrator starts reading aloud, so visitors know whose words are being quoted. For an exhibit that plays on a loop, display the interview title alongside the captions so someone arriving midway can place the story.
documents.rewrite:
Think about what a visitor needs to understand a pause or a change of voice. If both speakers break off to listen to a train whistle, a short caption naming the sound helps explain their reaction. Do the same for other sounds when they matter to the exchange. As soon as the narrator begins reading from a letter or diary, use the captions to introduce the passage and identify whose words the visitor is hearing.

Choose line breaks that follow the phrasing of the sentence, and put each person's given name and surname on the same line so visitors can read them at a glance. Have a reviewer watch an interview from beginning to end on mute and mark any answer that seems to have no lead-in. In a looping exhibit, keep the interview title visible beside the captions so people can identify the story even if they come in halfway through. Visitors who catch an error can help staff locate it if the correction slip prompts them for the interview title and the time on the player.

documents.original:
Have a host meet people at the door and offer to walk them over to the lesson, sparing a first-time visitor the search for a familiar face. Model both a friendly invitation and a friendly decline during the welcome. Guests get to hear how either answer can end comfortably. Announce the type of dance before the music starts so a beginner has time to decide whether to get up for it. Show an easy version of a turn that keeps both feet close to the floor, giving anyone who finds spinning uncomfortable a way through the figure.

Keep the teacher's face and feet well lit during demonstrations so people can use visual cues when the room is noisy. Invite people to chat briefly over a break with the music turned down. Someone who sat out a few songs can still get to know the group.
documents.rewrite:
Give newcomers someone to meet right away. A host at the door can offer to walk them to the lesson, so a first-time guest doesn't have to scan the room for someone they know. During the welcome, act out asking someone to dance and turning down a dance in a friendly way. Let people hear how comfortably the exchange can end whichever answer they give.

Before a song begins, tell the room which dance is coming up so beginners have a moment to decide whether to join in. Light the teacher's face as well as their feet during demonstrations, so people can follow by sight when it's hard to hear. For a turn, also teach a simple way to complete the figure with both feet low to the floor for anyone who finds spinning uncomfortable. Lower the music for a break and invite everyone to chat for a few minutes. A guest who has sat out several dances can still make some acquaintances that evening.

documents.original:
Welcome a loaf from a favorite neighborhood bakery. Someone without an oven can make an introduction every bit as interesting as a home baker's. Put blank ingredient cards beside the bread and leave room for fillings and toppings, which can be hard to identify from the crust. A stool at the exchange table gives anyone who tires of standing a chance to linger and talk to the bakers. Invite people to put a few words about a loaf's history beside it. Asking about a grandmother's skillet bread is an easier opening than introducing yourself to a room.

Set a basket of spare contributions aside for people who turn up empty-handed. A batch that didn't rise shouldn't have to keep a neighbor away. Show the suggested size of a swap portion with a real example near the door, saving newcomers the awkwardness of guessing what's fair.
documents.rewrite:
Make it clear that people can bring a loaf from a neighborhood bakery they love. A neighbor who has no oven might introduce everyone to a bread just as interesting as one baked at home. Keep some extra contributions in a basket for guests who arrive with nothing to swap, so a batch of dough that failed to rise needn't cost someone an evening with the group. At the entrance, display an actual piece of bread cut to the suggested swap size. It spares a newcomer the awkward guess about how much is fair.

Lay out blank ingredient cards alongside the loaves, with enough space to describe fillings and toppings that people may have trouble recognizing from the crust. Encourage contributors to leave a short note about the history of their bread, too. Asking a baker about their grandmother's skillet bread can feel easier than introducing yourself to everyone at once. A stool beside the exchange table lets someone who finds standing tiring stay a while and talk with the bakers.

documents.original:
Let a gardener contribute an unfinished pencil study near the front. A few searching lines make putting an imperfect mark in a public book feel easier. A small cardboard viewfinder helps someone faced with a whole border pick a patch of stems that fits on the page. Leave space for the plant's garden location beside a drawing, helping another visitor track down an intriguing seed head for a closer look. Keep a few pieces of scrap paper in the pencil tray for people who want to try a mark privately before committing it to the shared book.

An invitation to draw the fallen pods already on the table brings small details within reach without asking visitors to pick anything. Offer an occasional quiet drawing period before a garden tour, letting visitors who like to observe in silence try the books in company.
documents.rewrite:
Near the start of a book, invite a gardener to leave a pencil sketch that's still in progress. Seeing someone else's tentative lines can make it easier to risk an imperfect one on a page everyone will see. Tuck a few scraps of paper into the pencil tray for anyone who'd like to try out a stroke in private first.

For a visitor wondering how to fit a whole border on one page, offer a little cardboard viewfinder to frame a patch of stems. The fallen pods on the table make another good invitation to draw. Visitors can get close to the details without picking anything. Beside each sketch, leave room to say where in the garden the plant grows, so a reader taken with a particular seed head can find it and look more closely. Occasionally set aside quiet drawing time before a garden tour, so visitors who enjoy observing in silence can use the books together.

documents.original:
Let performers send word to one named contact if their journey is delayed, so the team can fill a gap while there's still time to use it. Reserve a rail for garments ready to go onstage, keeping them out of the alterations pile when the room is cleared at the end. Keep an easy-to-read clock within the fitter's sight so they can pace an appointment without repeatedly looking away from the performer. Mark borrowed pieces on the rail with the owner's alteration limits, saving a volunteer from shortening a hem that must be returned intact.

Circle any change that needs another fitting and agree on a return time with the wearer, while their schedule and the garment are both to hand. Write down the agreed priorities if there's more sewing than the team can finish, so a costume needed at tomorrow's rehearsal gets attention in time.
documents.rewrite:
Give performers one contact by name who can pass on word if they're held up on the way. The team may still have time to use the vacant slot. Put a clearly legible clock where the fitter can see it while attending to the performer, so they can keep the appointment on pace without repeatedly turning away.

On the rail, label each borrowed piece with the alterations its owner allows. A volunteer can then see that a hem has to go back exactly as it came before taking it up. Set aside a separate rail for stage-ready clothes so they won't get swept in with work awaiting alterations at the end of the night. Circle changes that call for a second fitting and settle the return time with the wearer while the garment is there and they have their schedule handy. If the sewing list outgrows the time available, record which jobs everyone agrees should come first so the costume for tomorrow's rehearsal gets worked on in time.

documents.original:
Keep a couple of tables for games where spoken questions are welcome, so a learner can ask about a move without guessing whether their opponent minds. Place a demonstration board in a corner away from active games, giving a helper room to show a position without gathering a crowd around someone else's match. Silence the beeps on communal clocks so the end of one game doesn't break a neighboring player's concentration. Give children who want to practise piece movement a set of their own, so they can explore how a knight jumps without borrowing from a live game.

Keep the sightline from the entrance to the tables open, allowing visitors to see whether the room is busy before walking through the playing area. Give players a quiet heads-up before closing time so a beginner still learning to judge game length can agree on a stopping point with their opponent.
documents.rewrite:
From the doorway, visitors should be able to see how busy the tables are before they step into the playing area, so keep that view clear. Dedicate a couple of tables to games where it's fine to ask questions out loud. Someone learning can then ask about a move without having to work out whether their opponent will mind. A demonstration board in a corner away from games in progress lets a helper set up a position and talk it through without drawing people around somebody else's match.

Give children who want to work on moving the pieces a set they can use themselves. They can try out the knight's jump without taking pieces from a game in progress. Turn off the beeps on the shared clocks so players can keep concentrating when the game next to them ends. A quiet word to the players before the room closes gives a beginner who's still getting a feel for how long games take time to agree with their opponent on where to stop.
